idiom_name: std::format emitter functions (C++20) or ostream insertion
implementation_notes: C++ also ships no template engine, so the classic structure is a hand-written emitter that walks the model and writes to an ostream or builds strings with std::format. std::format checks the format string at compile time for constant expressions and throws std::format_error for invalid specifications, but runtime template text must go through std::vformat and loses that check; escaping is still the caller's job because formatting is not HTML-aware. Header-only engines (inja, ctemplate) can be embedded when real templates are needed, but the hand-written form stays justified for small fixed pages, log and mail fragments, and code paths where an extra dependency is not acceptable.
pitfalls: The compile-time check disappears for runtime format strings: std::vformat accepts page text and reports a std::format_error only when the string is already being rendered, which is the classic format-string failure.
out << value writes raw bytes - escaping has to happen on the value before insertion, and each insertion point is a place to forget it.
Iterators, string_views and C-strings handed to a stream must outlive the emission; mutating the container while emitting yields dangling references with no engine to copy values for you.

std::format is C++20: older toolchains need fmtlib (with observable differences such as locale handling), and shipping a pages-as-strings template layer on top is the moment to justify the dependency.
